newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN CRISIS HITS GEORGI DIMITROV'S VILLAGE.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN CRISIS HITS GEORGI DIMITROV'S VILLAGE.

text.p: Bulgaria's economic crisis has not spared the once-prosperous birthplace of the founder of the communist state, Georgi Dimitrov.
The village, idyllically sited among wooded hills southwest of Sofia, boomed in the 1970s and 1980s as a pilgrimage site for every dignitary or East bloc tour group visiting Bulgaria.
Today its streets are deserted apart from three teenage boys riding bicycles on the square in front of a giant statue of Dimitrov, Bulgaria's equivalent to Lenin.
"It's the crisis keeping everyone at home," said Zdravko Nikolov, who owns the village cafe and declares himself a monarchist, supporting the return of exiled King Simeon. "No one has money."
Inflation estimated at 100 percent for February alone has eroded salaries. The average monthly state wage of 20,000 levs is worth about $10.
Kovachevtsi's school closed last month because price rises meant the daily bus fare from the town of Pernik added up to more than the teachers' salaries.
"For a while they hitchhiked, but then they gave up," said Valentin Manolov, one of about a dozen pupils who had been due to graduate this year.
The 1,000 villagers have also suffered from the bread and fuel shortages affecting the rest of the country.
"It's misery like we have never seen before," said Nikolov. "People have nothing to eat."
Metodi Krustev, Kovachevtsi's Socialist mayor, said villagers were receiving no more than 150 grammes of bread per day and the municipality had no fuel, but there was nothing he could do.
"This is not within my powers, I can do nothing, I cannot solve the country's problems," he said.
Communist-era visitors ensured jobs for the whole village and unemployment has soared since the end of one-party rule.

"Almost no one comes here now," said the receptionist in the town's chilly hotel, where the party general secretary's suite is still full of books celebrating the achievements of Dimitrov and longtime communist leader Todor Zhivkov.

Clients drinking coffee in Nikolov's cafe under a poster of King Simeon said that while nowadays they supported the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), they were grateful to Dimitrov for putting Kovachevtsi on the map.
Dimitrov emigrated to Moscow after the failure of a 1923 communist uprising and became a senior member of the Comintern, or Communist International.

He conducted his own defence at his Leipzig show trial on charges of setting fire to the German Reichstag in 1933, and after World War Two he was prime minister of the Peoples Republic of Bulgaria from 1945 until his death in 1949.

Dimitrov's body was removed from its Sofia mausoleum in 1990 after the end of one-party rule and quietly cremated. The building lies empty but is coveted by Sofia museums for its climate-control systems.

Nikolov estimated the people of Kovachevtsi were split equally between supporters of the UDF and of the ex-communist Bulgarian Socialist Party, who won elections in 1994 but were forced out of power last month by 30 days of mass protests. General elections are due on April 19.
"The communists are good only at taking care of themselves, they proved that by their rule," he said.
"We have waited so long, we can wait a bit longer. In two years, we hope things will change. If the UDF does half of what it promises it will be a success."
